title: The tentmaker
hookLine: Paul supports himself making tents while he travels (Acts 18:3)

lines: A COUPLE WITH THE SAME TRADE.
cards: The book of Acts is full of riots, shipwrecks and prison doors. Then, in Corinth, it slows down long enough to mention a job.

A traveling teacher arrives in the city and finds a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, lately come from Italy. They share a trade. So he moves in with them and goes to work: a bench, his hands, the day's labor.
Then, every sabbath, he goes to the synagogue to reason with whoever will listen. The man is Paul, and the book that tells his travels pauses to name his day job.

teach.h: OF THE SAME CRAFT, HE WROUGHT.
teach.b: First, the verse itself, in the King James Bible: "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." Wrought is the old word for worked.
Paul isn't visiting a workshop. He's in it. Second, why he did it.
Later in Acts, saying goodbye to friends from Ephesus, Paul holds up his hands: "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me."

In his own letters he says he had a right to be supported by the people he taught, and chose not to use it, so that nothing would hinder the gospel and he could offer it without charge. Third, what the text leaves out.
Acts doesn't describe the work at all: no tools, no customers, no hours. It names the trade and moves on. What it makes plain is that the teacher worked, and wasn't ashamed to say so.
Fourth, the people beside him. Aquila and Priscilla aren't just landlords. In Acts and in Paul's letters they appear again as teachers and friends, partners in the work as much as in the trade.
Some Christians today borrow the word itself.

teach.h: THE MESSAGE FREE, HIS OWN WAY PAID.
teach.b: They call someone a tentmaker when they carry their faith into an ordinary job and pay their own way, rather than being paid to preach.
Paul's letters also thank the church at Philippi for gifts sent to him, so he did sometimes accept help.

teach.h: BY THEIR OCCUPATION THEY WERE TENTMAKERS.
teach.b: But in Corinth, Acts shows him at the bench, working with his hands.

how: Some Christians call working an ordinary job while sharing their faith 'tentmaking', after Paul in Acts 18.

Paul's trade, which paid his way while he taught

games.q: who's who in Corinth — tap the pairs.
p: a couple of the same craft

s: Acts says Paul worked a trade while he traveled and taught
Acts 18:3: by their occupation they were tentmakers.

he says he had the right, and chose not to use it.
Aquila and Priscilla appear only as Paul's landlords

games.q: you're Paul, arriving in Corinth with a message to share and a living to earn. what do you do?
o: ask the synagogue to support you.
find people of your trade and go to work.
wait for followers to offer you a home.
games.why: Acts says he found Aquila and Priscilla, of the same craft, lived with them and worked, and taught on the sabbath.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that someone else quietly pays for or does for you, a ride, a bill, a meal, a chore that's drifted onto someone else's plate, and just notice it, with no guilt.
Then ask what one piece of it you could take back this week, and breathe with that. If you pray, you can offer your hands and their work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: The tentmaker. Paul's trade, according to Acts: working with Aquila and Priscilla, paying his own way while he taught. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: work with my hands. The message free, his own way paid. Until tomorrow.
